en: The Sūtra on the Simile of the Ants, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlaguṇabhadra, Imperially Appointed Court Attendant, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, who was conferred the purple robe, under imperial decree.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had emitted a great radiance that shone everywhere, he addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying: "You should know:
once there was a colony of ants that emitted smoke at night and blazed with fire during the day."
A certain brāhmaṇa, having seen this matter, spoke these words:
"If there were one who held a sharp and keen sword, he would surely be able to break up and disperse that gathering."
Having spoken thus, he next saw a large tortoise.
That brahmin also spoke these words:
"If there were one who held a sharp and keen blade, they would surely be able to destroy it."
Next he saw various *śukti* insects; next he saw a leech; next he saw various *asīsuṇa* insects; next he saw a great serpent; next he saw a *nāḍīpātra* insect; and next he saw a *kukkuṭa* insect.
When that brahmin saw those various insects, it was all as previously described.
Finally, he saw a great dragon.
The brahmin said:
“As I have seen it, what is the meaning of this matter?
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can fully understand it.
He immediately went to a bhikṣu and related the aforementioned matter in detail, further saying:
“Bhikṣu! On this matter, please inquire of the Buddha for me, so that my doubts may be cleared away.
As the Buddha explains it, I shall remember and uphold it.”
Why is this? Bhikṣus!
Among the gods, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas in this world, I do not see anyone who could question the Buddha on this matter; therefore, their various doubts cannot be cleared away and resolved.

Then that bhikṣu, acting exactly as he had been told, came to where I was. Upon arrival, he prostrated at my feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and after recounting the matter in detail, he further asked:
"Regarding the anthill seen by the brahmin, what is its significance?"
Why is it that smoke issues forth at night and fire blazes during the day?
Furthermore, one sees great tortoises, jellyfish, leeches, *asīsuna* insects, great serpents, *nudapatha* insects, *śakavāṭa* insects, and great dragons.
What kind of phenomena are all these that are seen?
Furthermore, who exactly is that brahmin?
For what reason is he called "Sharp Blade Shatterer"?
"May the Buddha please explain this for us! "O bhikṣus!
At that time, I said to those bhikṣus:"
"The gathering of ants is the aggregate body of the five skandhas of all sentient beings.
The smoke issuing forth at night is the arising of various vitarkas and vicāras within sentient beings."
The fire burning during the day represents the bodily and vocal actions that sentient beings initiate according to their discursive thoughts and investigations.
The great tortoise represents the five hindrances, which are defiled phenomena.
The jellyfish-like insect is anger and resentment;
the leech-like insect is stinginess and envy;
the *asīsuna* insect is the phenomena of the five desires.
The snake is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *nūdapatha* worm is doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The *kukūla* worm is pride (*māna*).
The dragon is none other than the arhats; the brahmin is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
and the sharp-witted one is the person possessed of wisdom.
"The sword is wisdom; 'shattering and dispersing' is the initiation of the superior practice of diligence. "O Bhikṣus!"
What do you think?

To speak briefly of those perceived characteristics, they are the bodies of all sentient beings—the aggregates of the five skandhas—born from the impurities of parents as the *kalala* and so forth; composed of the four great elements, they are false and illusory forms, coarse, evil, inferior, and weak, an accumulation of suffering and affliction that is ultimately subject to destruction.

Yet sentient beings are unable to awaken to this; throughout day and night they give rise to discursive thoughts and investigations, performing unwholesome actions of body and speech. They are shrouded by the five hindrances and afflictions, becoming addicted to the five sensual desires, increasing ignorance, and giving rise to a mind of pride. They harbor doubt and indecision regarding the noble Dharma, and in every thought-moment they give rise to anger, stinginess, and envy, seeking no liberation.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desires to cause all those with wisdom to arouse diligent practice, cultivate insight, sever all afflictions, and proceed toward the realization of the noble fruit.
"O bhikṣus! Since you have exhausted all outflows and realized the fruit of arhatship, you are said to be like nāgas.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!"

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past and future, out of compassion and for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, desiring to cause them to sever all afflictions and proceed toward the realization of the noble fruits, have extensively expounded this meaning for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Today, I too, like all the Buddhas, have proclaimed this for your sake on this very occasion.
You bhikṣus! Bear this matter in mind;

in solitary places such as wildernesses, empty dwellings, mountain valleys, beneath trees, rocky caves, or hermitages, contemplate it with focused thought and examine its meaning. Do not be negligent or give rise to a regressive mind, but likewise explain and instruct it to others, leading them all to practice it so that they may attain great benefit and happiness.

When the Blessed One had thus spoken to the bhikṣus, all the bhikṣus received it with faith and acceptance. This concludes the *Anta-upamā-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Ant Metaphor) as taught by the Buddha.
